title: Additive privacy cost for adversarial bandits
formal: Does there exist a pure centrally \(\varepsilon\)-differentially private adversarial-bandit algorithm, absolute constants \(C,p\ge0\), and a finite nonnegative function \(F(K,\varepsilon)\), independent of the horizon, such that for every \(K\ge2\), \(T\ge1\), \(0<\varepsilon\le1\) and oblivious loss array, its expected regret is at most \[C\sqrt{KT}\,(\log(2+KT))^p+F(K,\varepsilon)(\log(2+T))^p?\] This is the broad additive-separation question; no particular polynomial dependence of \(F\) is required.
definitions:
Before play, the adversary fixes \(\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_T)\), where \(\ell_t\in[0,1]^K\). At round \(t\), the learner chooses an action \(I_t\in[K]\) using its own randomness and only the past actions and observed losses \((I_s,\ell_s(I_s))\), \(s<t\). It then observes the single loss \(\ell_t(I_t)\), not the other entries. Its expected regret is \[R_T(\ell)=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(I_t)\right]-\min_{i\in[K]}\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(i).\] The comparator is one fixed best action in hindsight; the loss array is not sampled from a stochastic model.

Two input loss arrays are neighbors when all rows but one agree; the differing row may change all K entries. Only the action transcript \((I_1,\ldots,I_T)\) is public. Pure central privacy requires, for every neighboring pair \(\ell,\ell'\) and every \(E\subseteq[K]^T\), \(\Pr[A(\ell)\in E]\le e^\varepsilon\Pr[A(\ell')\in E]\). There is no additive privacy failure parameter. Raw observed losses and internal state are not public outputs. The learner is trusted to access the observed losses centrally; local privatization of each observation is a stronger restriction absent here.

The same finite algorithm accepts K, T and the privacy parameter; knowing the horizon is permitted. No running-time bound is imposed. The exponent p and leading constant C must be independent of K, T and privacy. F may depend arbitrarily, but finitely, on K and privacy and must be specified in a positive solution. In particular, privacy cannot enter a coefficient multiplying the square-root-in-T term. Only a fixed power of the logarithm of the horizon is allowed in the additive term. This explicit broad convention retains the imported question without choosing an unsupported preferred dependence such as K divided by privacy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of pure privacy and the uniform regret bound, including the function F and absolute constants, or a Lean-checked refutation of this broad additive-separation statement. Bounds for stochastic losses, full-information feedback, approximate privacy or only restricted algorithm families do not settle it. A multiplicative privacy factor in the leading square-root term does not meet the stated separation.
context:
Asi, Raman and Talwar define privacy with respect to changing one time-indexed loss vector and observing the action sequence. Their algorithm improves the multiplicative privacy dependence of adversarial-bandit regret.

Section 5 asks whether horizon and privacy can be separated additively and proves barriers for specified algorithm families. Those restrictions do not amount to an impossibility theorem for every centrally private bandit algorithm.
why: This asks whether privacy adds a separate cost or fundamentally multiplies the difficulty of adversarial learning.

import_provenance.original_title: An additive privacy cost for adversarial bandits
import_provenance.original_statement: For K-armed bandits with an oblivious adversary and central ε-differential privacy, can expected regret match the nonprivate O(√(KT)) term plus a privacy penalty independent of T up to logarithms? Talwar’s joint 2025 algorithm instead has a multiplicative 1/√ε cost, and its lower-bound discussion leaves unrestricted algorithms open.

sentences: The learner selects actions while seeing only the losses of its chosen actions.
An adversary fixes bounded losses before play, and changing one round must barely change the distribution of public actions.
The target separates a privacy-independent square-root horizon term from an additive privacy cost with only logarithmic horizon growth.
The source improves multiplicative privacy dependence and gives barriers limited to particular algorithm families.
Resolving the question would identify whether central privacy inherently changes the leading adversarial learning rate.
